stem: Shape s = new Circle(3); s.Area(); Whose Area body runs?
options: Circle's - the runtime looks at the REAL type
explanation: Dynamic dispatch: the declared type says what you may CALL; the runtime type decides which BODY runs. That is polymorphism.

stem: TotalArea sums s.Area() over a Shape[]. You add a new Pentagon class. What changes in TotalArea?
options: It must be recompiled with a flag
explanation: Polymorphism lets old code call new code: Pentagon brings its own Area, and TotalArea never knew about specific shapes in the first place.

stem: To replace a parent's method behaviour properly, the parent and child need which keywords?
options: virtual on the parent, override on the child
explanation: Both ends are explicit in C# - a deliberate contrast with Java. No virtual = cannot override; no override = you are hiding, not replacing.
new HIDES rather than replaces: which method runs depends on the DECLARED type of the variable. Through a Base variable, Base.Speak runs. Almost always a bug - use override.

stem: public abstract double Area(); in Shape means:
options: Every concrete subclass must supply an Area body, and Shape itself cannot be instantiated
explanation: abstract = requirement without implementation. The compiler enforces that every concrete child overrides it.

stem: public override string Send(string m) => base.Send(m) + " !!!"; What does base.Send do?
options: Calls the PARENT's version, letting the child extend rather than replace
Calls the first version ever written
explanation: base.Method() reaches one level up the hierarchy - decorate the parent's behaviour instead of duplicating it.

options: Printing and interpolation use it - your object gets a readable form everywhere at once
explanation: $"{shape}" and Console.WriteLine(shape) both call ToString. One override, readable output everywhere - the most useful override there is.

stem: Replacing 'switch (shape.Type)' with virtual Area() methods mainly buys you:
options: New shapes need NO edits to existing code
explanation: The switch must be found and edited for every new shape - and every place like it. Virtual dispatch puts the knowledge with the type. (Pattern switches have their place too - 4.6.)

options: At compile time, from the argument types
explanation: Overloading (same name, different parameters) is compile-time; overriding (virtual/override) is run-time. When people say polymorphism they usually mean the latter.

stem: You write override on a method whose parent version is not virtual. What happens?
options: Compile error - there is nothing to override
explanation: C# refuses: override requires a virtual or abstract member. This explicitness prevents accidental hiding.
